newsitem.title: UK: Hague hopes to rally Scottish Conservatives.
newsitem.headline: Hague hopes to rally Scottish Conservatives.

text.p: Britain's new opposition Conservative leader William Hague hopes on Friday to rally his party's Scottish wing which is still reeling after failing to win a seat in the May 1 general election.

Hague's address will wind up the annual Scottish Conservative conference amid disputes over the disastrous election showing and the party's stance on the Labour government's planned referendum on devolving powers to a separate Scottish parliament.
Opposition to any change in the 300-year-old link with England was a major factor in the Conservatives' election drubbing in Scotland.
Hague reiterated that opposition on a fleeting visit to Glasgow and Edinburgh last Saturday.

Former cabinet minister Peter Lilley gave the same message at a private pre-conference meeting on Thursday. He stressed, however, that Conservative policies must have "a Scottish dimension tailored to the needs, opportunities and hopes of the Scottish people".
Lilley said Conservative policies had restored the British economy and that Labour became electable only by adopting them wholesale.
Many Scottish Conservative activists regard a devolved parliament as inevitable and say the party should work for maximum representation in it.

Opinion polls since the general election, when the Conservatives lost all 10 Scottish seats they held in the House of Commons, have shown the majority of Scots want their own parliament and that at least 25 percent of Conservatives are in favour.
Some grass-roots Conservative workers attribute the election failure that virtually wiped them off the political map in Scotland to a perception of the party as English-dominated.

This was reinforced by Hague's victory in the Conservative leadership election this month to replace former prime minister John Major. Scots had no vote in the contest as they had no members of parliament.
Several pro-devolution party members are in effect boycotting the Perth conference.
"I refuse to give blind homage to a leader whom I did not have any part in electing," said Brian Meek.
"I know little of his policies other than his distaste for devolution and his suspicions about Europe. Neither of these brought us rip-roaring success."
Meek, chairman of the Conservative group on Edinburgh city council, is one of only 82 Conservatives among the 1245 local councillors in Scotland.

He claims the one-day conference -- a far cry from the rousing two- or three-day events used by former prime minister Margaret Thatcher to launch her most adventurous policies -- has been "stitched up" by the present leadership. Meek is attending the Wimbledon tennis championships instead.
Other activists suggest Conservatives will only regain support by forming a separate Scottish party that elects its own leadership free of control by Central Office in London.
Hague has had to appoint three Scots elected by English constituencies to speak on Scottish affairs in the House of Commons.
